proof_skeleton_nl: Construct the graph of all valid one-coordinate genus-raising moves. The difficult combinatorial part is to verify Hall's condition. This is reduced to lexicographic initial segments by a compression lemma, and then proved on those initial segments by a separate neighborhood lower bound. Hall's theorem then produces a matching from every x in K_{m,g} to a distinct y in K_{m,g+1}, which is exactly the required injection.

steps.derives: For the fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, both K_{m,g} and K_{m,g+1} are finite. Therefore the one-step increment graph G_{m,g}, whose left vertices are K_{m,g}, whose right vertices are K_{m,g+1}, and whose edges are x~y exactly when y differs from x by increasing one coordinate by 1, is a finite bipartite graph.

Every x in K_{m,g} has at least one neighbor in G_{m,g}: choose an index r where x_r is minimal, then L2 gives x+e_r in K_{m,g+1}, so x is adjacent to x+e_r. This records the basic local extension property of the graph.

Let A be an arbitrary subset of K_{m,g}, and set n = |A|. Let I_n be the set of the n lexicographically smallest elements of K_{m,g}. By L4, the neighborhood of A in G_{m,g} satisfies |N(A)| >= |N(I_n)|. Thus, to prove Hall's inequality for A, it is enough to prove it for the corresponding initial segment I_n.

By L3, the initial segment I_n has at least n neighbors in G_{m,g}, so |N(I_n)| >= n. Combining this with A3 gives |N(A)| >= |N(I_n)| >= n = |A|. Therefore the arbitrary subset A satisfies Hall's inequality.

Because A was an arbitrary subset of K_{m,g}, the conclusion of A4 shows that every subset A of the left vertex set K_{m,g} satisfies |N(A)| >= |A|. Hence the bipartite graph G_{m,g} satisfies Hall's condition on its left side.
steps.trivial_justification: This is direct universal generalization from the arbitrary subset A considered in A4.

steps.derives: Applying Hall's theorem L5 to the finite bipartite graph G_{m,g} yields an injective function f:K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} such that each x in K_{m,g} is adjacent to f(x) in G_{m,g}. In particular, f really has codomain K_{m,g+1} and is injective.

Set J_{m,g} = f. Then J_{m,g} is an injective function from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}. Therefore, for the given integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, there exists an injective function J_{m,g} from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}.
steps.trivial_justification: This is just renaming the injective map f obtained in A6.
